title: A few months ago I said here that "Claude, build me a profitable strategy" does not work. I re-tested it with Fable 5.2, three ways. I was half wrong.
author: LeastTangelo6022
selftext:
My honest update after testing the new Claude on trading.



A few months ago I posted here about a year of vibe trading with AI. One of my "what does NOT work" points was this:



"Claude, build me a profitable strategy." It grabs some data, overfits, tests 50 hypotheses and hands you survivorship bias with a smile.



Then Fable 5.2 came out and everyone started posting what it one shotted. Games, 3D rooms, whole apps. So we asked it for something you can't fake with a nice demo. A BTC strategy. Three ways.



Before the numbers: I build Trigr, the backtester we used in rounds 1 and 3. Read everything with that in mind. Round 2 is the one without it.



**Round 1: one prompt, connected to the backtester**

\> One line: "Build me a great strategy."

\> Eight minutes later it had a BTC breakout strategy on the 4 hour chart. No leverage, no tuning, one backtest.

\> The last year of prices was locked away. The strategy never saw it, and ran on it once. BTC fell about 30% in that year. The strategy made +16.9%.



**Round 2: the model alone**

\> Clean chat, same ask, no tools from us. I expected a nice sounding guess. We got a research lab.

\> It found years of price data on its own. It wrote its own backtest engine. It ran about 7,000 backtests in 35 minutes. Then it handed us a strategy with a warning label it wrote itself: "Partly fitted. Expect live results well below the backtest."

\> We rebuilt its rules on the same engine as round 1 to compare. It beat round 1. More return, better Sharpe.

\> The version without my product won. I excpected that since we have strong overfit guards that counts iterations and prevent data leaks and look ahead.



**Round 3: let it tune its own strategy**

\> Six tries, a few minutes. Raising the size cap gave the biggest jump. Making shorts pickier gave the best version. Faster and slower entries both made it worse. Two of the six looked better overall and still got flagged as high risk, one of them because its last year turned negative.



**The numbers**

BTC, 1 Jan 2020 to Nov 2026, all three on the same engine, after fees, slippage and real funding. These are backtests.

\- Round 1, one shot: +512.5%, Sharpe 1.07, max drawdown 25.5%, size 1x, 1 backtest

\- Round 2, alone: +815.0%, Sharpe 1.24, max drawdown 29.9%, size up to 1.74x, about 7,000 backtests

\- Round 3, tuned: +1,348.5%, Sharpe 1.30, max drawdown 32.3%, size up to 2.06x, 6 more tries

\- Just holding BTC: about +913%, with a drop of about 77% on the way



**Where I was wrong**

The model alone is a real researcher now. Nobody told it to find data or build an engine.

It doesn't hand you survivorship bias with a smile anymore. It told us its own strategy was partly fitted. Before, I had to ask "are you sure the results?" to get that.

It still overfits. It just does it faster. In July I complained about 50 hypotheses. This time it ran about 7,000 backtests to pick one strategy.

  
**Where I was right**

It guessed the costs. On its own engine the round 2 strategy looked about twice as good. The real funding cost was several times bigger than its guess. On the tuned version, slippage and funding alone take the backtest from +2,057% to +1,348%.



Tuning is where it gets dangerous. Six tries took the return from +815% to +1,348%. Sharpe only went from 1.24 to 1.30. A lot of the extra return is just bigger size, with the deepest drawdown of the three. And its last year got worse, from +31.0% to +24.6%.



**--> Reality check:** only round 1 faced a year it had never seen. The other two were shaped with that year already in view. So the smallest number on the board is the only one I half trust.



The pattern is the same as in July. AI accelerates the process, you own the validation. The model got a lot better at research. The backtest is still the most optimistic number you will ever see.



None of these has traded live. All three are running on paper from today, which is the only data none of them has seen. Time beats backtests. I'll post the scores here, good or bad.



Has anyone else re-run an old "AI can't do this" test on the new model? And if you let an agent tune a strategy, how many tries do you allow before you stop trusting the result?

comments.author: tymerch
comments.body: you cant build strategy with ai, it will overfit it

comments.author: AoideusWasBanned
comments.body:
The number I'd look at is the one you already flagged: tuning took Sharpe from 1.24 to 1.30 while the last year got worse, from +31.0% to +24.6%. When return moves a lot and the risk-adjusted part barely moves, the search is mostly fitting noise.

Part of the jump is also just size going from 1x to 2.06x, with drawdown going from 25.5% to 32.3%. I'd compare the three rounds at the same exposure before calling round 3 better.

With ~7,000 backtests the best one will look good even if nothing is there. A deflated Sharpe that counts every backtest as a trial helps, or simpler, keep the last 12-18 months locked away and let the agent see it only once at the very end. Tbh I don't think a fixed try limit works well, I'd stop trusting it the moment the locked period doesn't hold up.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: round 2 is where I'd press. it found its own price data and ran about 7,000 backtests, so unless its download stopped before your locked year, that year isn't locked for round 2, and beating round 1 on it means less. holding back a stretch the strategy never sees is something I put into Quantradin too, I built it for American stocks and their options, no crypto. quantradin.com. maybe I missed it, but what date range did round 2 actually pull?

comments.author: Ok_Map5721
comments.body:
Biggest factor in my experience: search. Lots of configs and tickers get tried on one short window and only the best gets written up. Best of N pure noise already shows t ≈ √(2·ln N), so 1,000 tries look like a t ≈ 3.7 "edge".

LLM-specific problem: the model has read about the period it's backtested on, so a pre-cutoff backtest is never really out of sample.

Before I'd believe an agent has alpha: rules, prompts and model version hashed before the test; a forward window after the training cutoff, scored once; point-in-time universe; real bid/ask, fees and funding; buy-and-hold at the same exposure as the benchmark; random-entry placebos; and the total number of variants tried, reported.
